entities.summary:
The Social Democratic Party (Partido Social Democrata, PSD) is a pivotal political institution in Portugal, founded on May 6, 1974, amid the revolutionary fervor following the Carnation Revolution, which ended decades of authoritarian rule under the Estado Novo regime. As a centre-right party, it emerged as a significant player in shaping post-revolutionary Portuguese politics, advocating for democratic governance, economic liberalization, and European integration. Key figures in its establishment include Francisco Sá Carneiro, who became the party's first prominent leader, representing a shift in political ideology towards democratic principles and market-oriented policies in Southern Europe.

The party played a crucial role in Portugal's transition to democracy, participating in the drafting of the new constitution and influencing the country's accession to the European Economic Community in 1986. Throughout the late 20th century, the PSD alternated in power with the Socialist Party, illustrating the dynamic nature of Portuguese politics. Noteworthy achievements include implementing significant economic reforms and social policies aimed at modernizing the nation, while facing challenges such as economic crises and internal party divisions.

As the PSD navigated the complexities of coalition governments and shifting public sentiment, it contributed to the establishment of a stable democratic framework in Portugal, which has had lasting impacts on governance and policy-making in the region. The party's legacy includes its ongoing influence on political discourse and policy in Portugal, as well as its role in fostering a pro-European sentiment among Portuguese citizens. The PSD's evolution reflects broader trends in Southern Europe, where social democratic movements have adapted to changing socio-economic landscapes.
